party.description: The ACT Party (Rōpū ACT) is a right-wing libertarian and populist party that advocates free-market policies and reducing the role of government. It currently has 10  seats in parliament. ACT was formed in 1994 from the Association of Consumers and Taxpayers by former National MP Derek Quigly and former Labour minister of finance Roger Douglas. It has had seats in parliament since 1996 and has held the Epsom electorate since 2005. ACT gave support to the fifth National government from 2008 to 2017 through a confidence and supply agreement. The party is currently in government as part of the National-led coaltion.
party.name: ACT Party

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that pharmacists have capacity that GPs and other health services may not. Increasing the number of conditions that pharmacists can prescribe or provide care for without needing approval from a doctor or nurse will make it easier for people managing long-term conditions or those with straightforward sicknesses with clear diagnosis. This would reduce wait times for GPs and provide quicker care.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would list more sicknesses and ailments pharmacists are allowed to treat, including sore throats, tonsillitis, gout and period pain. There would be a protocol for when pharmacists should refer back to a doctor for treatment. Consultation fees would remain capped at $20 for most and $5 for Community Service Card holders.

citations.title: 'Your pharmacist should be your first stop', 6 August 2026 (accessed 06 August 2026)

policies.statement: Allow pharmacists to treat more sicknesses and conditions

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that removing the rule that prevents a single person or entity from owning more than five pharmacies would make it easier to open new pharmacies. Changing other rules about pharmacy locations, licenses and qualifications for pharmacists would make it easier to open and staff pharmacies anywhere in the country.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: The party would change regulatory settings to implement the reforms. Online prescription e-lockers can be used to help those in rural areas access medication when pharmacies may have limited opening hours.

citations.title: 'Your pharmacist should be your first stop', 6 August 2026 (accessed 06 August 2026)
'ACT will drive down costs for farmers', 22 October 2026 (accessed 23 October 2026)

policies.statement: Remove some rules around pharmacy locations, ownership and licences

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that most people who are released from prison for burglary end up in prison again within two years. By making longer sentences without parole mandatory, burglary will be prevented and people with convictions for burglary will reoffend less.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would make receiving a third conviction of burglary or a single conviction for three counts of burglary would require a minimum sentence of three years in prison, with no home detention, parole or early release. Judges would use discretion for the length of sentence, between three and ten years. An aggravated burglary would count both for three strikes for violent crime and three strikes for burglary.

citations.title: 'Three Strikes for Burglary', undated (accessed 07 August 2026)

policies.statement: Require a minimum three-year sentence for anyone convicted of burglary three times

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that many medications for conditions like cancer are publicly funded in Australia but not in NZ. The public drug funding system Pharmac, is not receiving enough funding to keep up. Paying for medication can reduce pressure elsewhere in the health system by helping people manage their health conditions effectively.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would increase funding for Pharmac by 1 percent per year until 2033, from the current base of 4.9 percent of the health budget. More medications on Pharmac's "options for investment" list would become available to New Zealanders. A sustainable funding option would mean Pharmac can spend money on drugs for more health conditions.  This party estimates that this policy would cost over $4bn over 7 years.

citations.title: 'Closing the Medicines Gap', 26 July 2026 (accessed 07 August 2026)

policies.statement: Increase the percentage of the health budget spent on Pharmac to over 10 percent by 2033

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that in areas of forest and mountains where people want to hunt, there are "no-fly" and "no-landing" areas for helicopters with no clear reasoning. In areas where helicopters are the fastest way in, access restrictions should be justified with obvious safety or conservation reasons.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would allow the Game Council to designate helicopter landing sites, and restrict commercial venison operators by animal gender when necessary, leaving trophy stags for hunters. DOC would be required to use public tests to designate where aircraft could land, and would not have any say in which types of helicopters were used. The Outdoors Access Commission would be asked to make hunting access a priority in its work programme.

citations.title: 'Open the Backcountry', undated (accessed 07 August 2026)
'ACT will drive down costs for farmers', 22 October 2026 (accessed 23 October 2026)

policies.statement: Increase the areas of conservation land which can be accessed by helicopter for hunting

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that previous policy directions have required that public agencies should allocate services based on individual need and value, rather than race. Universities should be included in this directive too, as universities are independent but largely funded by the taxpayer. Grants or donations from private money would be exempt from this requirement.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would amend the Education and Training Act, adding language preventing benefits or support being offered on the basis of race of ethnicity. This would include scholarships, accommodation support, designated spaces in tertiary institutions and any other types of support. Universities would still be able to confer scholarships based on academic merit, need, geographic location, economic circumstances or disability.

citations.title: 'Equal Treatment at Universities', undated (accessed 10 August 2026)

policies.statement: Prevent universities from allocating support of any kind based on ethnicity

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that pets are being threatened and abused to coerce people in family violence situations and prevent them from leaving. Research shows half of victims delay leaving a violent situation because they are concerned about their pets. Criminalising the abuse of animals in this context will give Police more tools to protect victims. States in Australia and the US have enacted similar laws and New Zealand needs to do the same.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would amend the Crimes Act to make abusing a pet with the goal of coercion an offence punishable by a maximum seven years in prison. Protection orders would be strengthened to ensure offenders cannot control access to a pet and ensure pets are not left with abusers. Police would be required to record the presence of pets in a family violence situation and receive clear operational guidance around removing pets to a safe place if the animal is at risk of harm.

citations.title: 'Stop Coercion by Animal Abuse', undated (accessed 07 August 2026)

policies.statement: Make the abuse of a companion animal in a family violence situation a crime

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that New Zealand's dairy industry has a lower emissions footprint than the global average. Adding methane emissions from dairy farming to the Emissions Trading Scheme would make producing dairy more expensive and mean more dairy production happens in other countries. New Zealand should be increasing dairy production instead of reducing it to limit emissions. The Paris Agreement is not fit for purpose.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would continue to exclude emissions from the agriculture sector from the Emissions Trading Scheme. Agriculture would be permanently excluded. This policy would be part of a changed approach to New Zealand's commitments under the Paris Agreement.

citations.title: 'Paris Needs to Change', undated (accessed 11 August 2026)

policies.statement: Ensure agriculture is not part of the emissions trading scheme

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that carbon dioxide and methane both contribute to global heating. Carbon dioxide stays in the atmosphere longer than methane, which is largely produced by the dairy and sheep industries.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would rewrite NZ's Nationally Determined Contributions plan, which is required by the Paris Agreement. It would differentiate between the emissions caused by methane and carbon dioxide so that methane emissions do not have to be reduced by the same degree as carbon emissions. A "split gas approach" would calculate the emissions generated by carbon dioxide and methane differently. Carbon dioxide emissions would be reduced while methane levels could continue at current levels.

citations.title: 'Paris Needs to Change', undated (accessed 11 August 2026)

policies.statement: Count carbon dioxide and methane differently under emissions targets

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that people can disrupt hunters by stepping into the line of fire, or disturbing game birds with a drone. This should not happen if a hunter is following legal guidelines and safety protocols. While people are free to protest hunting, those protests should not place anyone at risk.  It says that currently there are no laws covering this situation which needs to change.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would create specific infringement offences for standing in the line of fire of a hunter, and for disturbing game birds with aircraft like drones or helicopters. These infringements would not apply if the hunter was not following the relevant laws and guidelines.

citations.title: 'Protect Lawful Hunting', undated (accessed 07 August 2026)
'ACT will drive down costs for farmers', 22 October 2026 (accessed 23 October 2026)

policies.statement: Make disrupting lawful hunters with drones or by standing in the line of fire an offence

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that there are twice as many security guards as police officers in New Zealand, but security guards don't have any legal authority. People who do not feel safe in shops buy online instead, impacting small businesses. Licencing trained and vetted security guards to remove people and use proportionate force when necessary would be good for businesses worried about crime. It would accompany current law reforms allowing people to make citizens arrests if no police are present.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would train vetted security guards; those who complete the training would be issued with a special licence. The licence would allow them to require a person's name an address to enter a premise; issue up to 3-year exclusion notices for a premise or premises; remove people who are threatening or breaching entry conditions; carry out safety searches individuals would have to consent to as a condition of entry; if necessary, use force, until the person complies or the police arrive. Licenced security professionals would have the ability to detain someone while waiting for the police.

citations.title: 'Keeping Public Spaces Safe', undated (accessed 07 August 2026)

policies.statement: Issue licences for security professionals to have more authority against intrusion or theft

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that legislation currently treats deer as pest animals to be exterminated rather than game animals to be hunted. The Game Council can advise DOC but does not make decisions. Hunters spend time in the area where these animals live and should be making decisions about what happens to game animals on conservation land.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would transfer responsibility for game animals from DOC to the Game Council. It would also give the Council more funding to recognise its further responsibilities.

citations.title: 'Hunter-led Game Management', undated (accessed 07 August 2026)
'ACT will drive down costs for farmers', 22 October 2026 (accessed 23 October 2026)

policies.statement: Give the Game Council responsibility for game animals on conservation land

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that game animals on NZ's conservation land are treated as pests which should be killed. However, these animals are valuable to many rural communities and hunters and should be treated as natural resources instead. Hunters can strike a balance between removing game animals to protect the natural environment and ensuring there are enough game for the future.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would change legislation to designate game animals and birds as natural resources rather than pests. Herds of New Zealand deer, which hunters appreciate, would be designated as specific "Herds of Special Interest" for protection. The whitetail deer on Stewart Island would be given this designation.

citations.title: 'Hunter-led Game Management', undated (accessed 07 August 2026)

policies.statement: Recognise introduced game species in law

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that in 2025, 38,000 WINZ hardship loans were issued to help families cover the cost of school uniforms, and in some cases the combined cost for school uniforms is over $1,000. Limiting state schools to just three branded school items will make uniforms more affordable for New Zealanders. Generic items such as socks would be available from low-cost retailers like The Warehouse or KMart. School uniforms can promote school culture but expensive uniforms don't improve educational outcomes, and similar policies in parts of Australia and the UK have been successful.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would limit state schools to three mandatory branded items as part of a uniform. Alternative, generic options for clothes like skirts, shirts, trousers and socks could be selected from low-cost retail stores. This policy would only apply to everyday items worn to school, not to more special items like branded clothing for sports teams.

citations.title: 'Affordable School Uniforms', undated (accessed 10 August 2026)

policies.statement: Limit the number of branded items in school uniforms to reduce costs

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that school transport rules are based on the nearest school. Parents who choose different schools for reasons like siblings being close together may not be able to use a school bus service. This is particularly difficult for families in rural areas. Allowing children to ride any school bus with space would make it easier for families.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would introduce a rule where a child living along an existing school bus route could use any available seat. If a bus route became full, another one would be provided by the Ministry of Education. Any extra funding would come from the education budget by cutting other spending.

citations.title: 'Let the Kid on the Bus ', undated

policies.statement: Allow children to take any passing school bus, not just buses specifically for one school

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that that DOC has a 30 percent maintenance shortfall and has issued more than 2,300 closure alerts since 2021. Volunteer groups carry out track and hut maintenance, but should receive funding for this over multiple years rather than applying annually. Creating a system for groups to receive biodiversity credits will incentivise further volunteer work in the hills.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would require DOC to give community groups the first opportunity for funding for maintenance on conservation land. Community groups would be allowed to sign multi-year contracts for work they are able to do. If biodiversity benefits were independently verified, groups including hunters would receive biodiversity credits. The Game Council and Deerstalkers Association would be formally represented when deciding how animals on conservation land were managed.

citations.title: 'Back the Volunteers', undated (accessed 07 August 2026)
'ACT will drive down costs for farmers', 22 October 2026 (accessed 23 October 2026)

policies.statement: Give volunteer groups more opportunities and funding for maintenance on conservation land

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that millions of tourists come to New Zealand, but these visitors can place pressure on local infrastructure. International visitors pay a levy that is collected by central government, but local government needs funding for infrustructure costs like roads and wastewater. Any new taxes or expenses should be very specifically targeted to where they are needed without making things more expensive for residents and ratepayers.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would use a data programme to determine where international visitors are staying. Each year, the central government would make an automatic annual payment of $1 for each night an international visitor spent in that council area. This dividend could replace some increases to rates which would otherwise pay for infrastructure upgrades. Based on 2026 nights, this would include $8.2m for Auckland, $4.9m for Queenstown and $2m for Rotorua.

citations.title: 'Local Tourism Dividend', undated (accessed 18 August 2026)
'ACT is supporting local tourism, not new taxes ', 14 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)
'Tourism Policy' (PDF), undated (accessed 18 August 2026)
'ACT sets the No New Taxes agenda', 8 September 2026 (accessed 11 September 2026)

policies.statement: Return $1 to local authorities for each night an international tourist spends in their area

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that it's important to support innovation in the NZ financial system. The party claims that cryptocurrency help businesses engage in the global market. The party argues that the government should regulate digital financial assets to facilitate smoother capital investment while ensuring consumer protection and legality. It wants to ensure legitimate businesses have access to banking and are not turned away due to the novel use of cryptocurrency.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value:
This party would establish clear legal and tax rules for cryptocurrency. Such regulation would define what regulated digital currency is. It would review NZ financial regulations to gauge whether current settings deny legitimate businesses access to banking. The party seeks to scale regulation by firm size. 

The party would allow smaller firms a license to experiment with cryptocurrency. This license would exist under government supervision.

citations.title: 'Unlocking New Zealand’s Digital Economy' (PDF), 27 August 2026 (accessed 28 August 2026)

policies.statement: Create a regulatory framework for the use of cryptocurrency

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that incentivise and provide stability for those seeking to invest in cryptocurrency for the long term.  The party says it wants to simplify and minimise tax compliance complications for everyday users.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would introduce exemptions for low-value purchases made using cryptocurrency. This party would apply exemptions for the first twelve months of investments that qualify as personal investments in cryptocurrency. Business investments would remain fully taxable.

citations.title: 'Unlocking New Zealand’s Digital Economy' (PDF), 27 August 2026 (accessed 28 August 2026)

policies.statement: Create tax exemptions for use of cryptocurrency

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that people need to be regularly living in NZ to be regarded as a permanent resident. They need to show an ongoing connection to NZ.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would remove the permanent resident visa category and instead change the resident visa to mandate residents to live 2 out of 5 years in NZ. Exemptions will exist for service members, employees of NZ-owned businesses, and certain family commitments.

citations.title: 'ACT’s New Immigration Policy To Put ‘Reside’ Back In ‘Resident’', 1 September 2026 (accessed 01 September 2026)

policies.statement: Add a physical presence test to permanent residents

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that voluntary student membership of student associations at universities has been undermined by compulsory 'service fees.' The party says these fees add costs for students that should be paid as they use the services. Instead, the party argues that service fees force students to fund union campaigns and media services that not all students support.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would change regulations so that services are offered as a menu. Students would then select what services they wish to use. This would prohibit compulsory service fees used to fund services traditionally funded by student unions/associations.

citations.title: 'ACT to campaign on making Student Services Fees voluntary', 10 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Make Student Service Fees voluntary

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that, to protect democratic majority rule, judges cannot be allowed to enable Treaty principles to go beyond what Parliament intended. Greater clarity in legislation and removing Treaty considerations would provide greater protection of individual property rights and prevent ethnicity-based equity measures.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value:
This party would add three principles to the Constitution Act. These would be that Parliament is the highest legal authority in NZ; the rule of law is fundamental; and all New Zealanders are equal before the law.  It would also insert property rights into the New Zealand Bill of Rights to ensure homes, farms, businesses and other property are protected.
Tikanga could be used in court only when it was relevant to a case, or where Parliament has expressly provided for it.

citations.title: 'One Law for All, One Future Together', undated (accessed 18 August 2026)
'Finish the settlements, wind up the Waitangi Tribunal' (PDF), 10 September 2026 (accessed 11 September 2026)
'One Law for All Policy' (PDF), 23 August 2026 (accessed 24 August 2026)

policies.statement: Scale back the use and effect of Treaty principles in legislation

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: The party says the only criterion for a person receiving publicly funded services should be need, rather than equity across different groups.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: The party would create a clear statutory duty that public services are delivered based on need, without group-based equity considerations changing the Public Service Act. Agencies would be required to comply with the principle as a matter of law, and decisions that breach it could be subject to judicial review.

citations.title: 'One Public Service for All ' (PDF), undated (accessed 18 August 2026)
'One public service for all', undated (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Remove ethnicity-based criteria for delivering public services

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that that group-based equity measures, such as hiring people of specific ethnic backgrounds, are unneeded. Group-based considerations cannot exist alongside merit-based recruitment.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would repeal group-based requirements on government departments as employers. It would repeal Section 73 of the Public Service Act, and its equivalent in the Crown Entities Act.

citations.title: 'One Public Service for All ' (PDF), undated (accessed 18 August 2026)
'One public service for all', undated (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Remove group-based equity measures from recruitment in the public sector

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that taxpayers' time and money should not be spent on cultural practices that some staff may not want to do, like prayers and karakia. The party says that cultural skills should only matter as part of a job if absolutely necessary and should not distract from the primary responsibility employees have. Employees should express cultural or spiritual practices like prayers or karakia outside of the workplace.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would prohibit cultural or spiritual practices in the workplace of public institutions. It would use a clear letter of expectations to the Public Service Commissioner and Cabinet to enforce the removal of cultural expectations.

citations.title: 'One Public Service for All ' (PDF), undated (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Prevent cultural practices from being used in the public service

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that countries with a similar population to NZ have fewer government ministries.Merging existing ministries can reduce duplication of responsibility. It says that government spending increases are associated with the number of ministers in a government.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would to reduce the number of ministries by over half with one senior minister responsible for more areas. Other minister positions that are cut will become junior minister roles below the senior minister.

citations.title: 'ACT unveils plan for radically simpler smaller government ', 28 June 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Reduce number of ministries into consolidated departments

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that many people need to get away from sickness benefits and into work. It claims that the country doesn't want to miss out on their potential.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would make all health and disability benefits subject to approval from an MSD-approved pool of designated doctors. The party would have assessments be made against clear, objective criteria, rather than leaving major long-term benefit decisions to discretion. Reassessment would begin with mental-health-related grants made after the pandemic. Other reassessments would be phased in with the new criteria for existing Jobseeker Support, health conditions or disabilities and Supported Living Payment.

citations.title: 'ACT announces policy to make benefits a hand-up, not a way of life', 28 June 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Restrict how many people recieve medical certification for health-related benefits

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that there is a need for greater fairness in the welfare system. Some beneficiaries spend money in ways that do not prepare them for work, such as gambling, alcohol and tobacco. The party argues that taxpayers should not fund the purchasing of products that set people back from potentially finding employment.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would require that people on a jobseeker benefit for 4 months be automatically shifted onto an electronic money management card system. Such a system would block expenses related to smoking, drinking, and gambling. Carve-outs and modified arrangements where money management would risk safety or block access to necessities.

citations.title: 'ACT announces policy to make benefits a hand-up, not a way of life', 28 June 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Monitor spending for jobseekers receiving a benefit for more than 4 months

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says it can take up to 3 years for complaints about worker conduct to reach an employer. The party claims that current checks only capture a snapshot in time and not ongoing accountability.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would create a Working with Children card. Eligibility for the card would take into account relevant criminal convictions, disciplinary findings and other records relating to children or child-related work. If a cardholder is charged with a disqualifying offence, their card could be suspended or revoked, and their employer notified. This would simplify the system for employers and ensure child safety mechanisms can react in real time.

citations.title: 'ACT will introduce smarter screening to improve child safety ', 17 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Create a "Working with Children" card

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that cancer is an issue that affects so many families. Cancer is New Zealand’s biggest killer. More than 30,000 New Zealanders are diagnosed each year; by 2044, that number is expected to exceed 45,000.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would build two centres, built in Christchurch and Auckland. These would be financed through public-private partnerships, charitable donations, existing Crown health investment and other private capital. The investment would be accompanied by a government-run independent philanthropic foundation to help secure additional investment.  This party estimates that this policy would cost 2 billion in baseline capital expenditure.

citations.title: 'ACT unveils plan for New Zealand’s first dedicated Cancer centre - Beyond Tomorrow', 21 August 2026 (accessed 24 August 2026)

policies.statement: Establish a public-private partnership to build two independent cancer centres.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that claims that VPNs are a key means of privacy protection for journalists, commercial, and personal information. The technology is part of modern cyber-security and should be accessible to the public.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would not allow VPN bans to be part of any coalition agreement. The party claims it would oppose any VPN ban included in legislation banning children from social media.

citations.title: 'Act will stop any VPN ban', 7 July 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Prevent any banning of VPNs

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that NZ is falling behind because innovative technology like driverless cars and drones available overseas remains illegal. It argues that NZ policy settings are not responsive to change and need greater flexibility. Results from these trials could to help bolster the evidence base for regulatory change.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would create an application process that would see a singular business be exempt from a particular regulation. The approval would state the safety conditions and how the result will be measured. The Ministry for Regulation would help to run the trials, and companies working in the fields of novel medical technology, drones for agricultural use or driverless cars would be invited to test out this technology.

citations.title: 'Innovation Trials', undated (accessed 10 August 2026)

policies.statement: Allow "innovation trials" for new technology not covered by NZ law

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that those on temporary work visas use infrastructure and should help fund its investment. The party claims its tax would raise $80m annually; the NZ temporary work visa would remain cheaper than in both the UK and Australia.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would add the tax on top of existing taxes. Such a process would be automated through the link between visas and employers.

citations.title: 'A Fair Contribution', undated (accessed 10 August 2026)

policies.statement: Establish a $6-a-day infrastructure surcharge to temporary work visas

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says it wishes to remove dangerous people from society. In addition, it aims to build greater trust in both law and order and immigration.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would deport Resident Visa holders convicted of offences carrying sentences of 10 years or more, irrespective of how long they have lived in the country. The party specifies that naturalised citizens would not be deported.

citations.title: 'Deport Serious Offenders', undated (accessed 07 August 2026)

policies.statement: Deport serious offenders who are not New Zealand citizens

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that that it is unfair for New Zealanders to fund benefits for people who've only recently committed to living and working in NZ. The party claims its change will prevent any encouragement of welfare dependency among new arrivals.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: The party would have residence-class visa holders made ineligible for all welfare benefits for the first five years. The party claims it would do so by changing the eligibility criteria that presently permit residence-class visa holders to access welfare benefits.

citations.title: 'Deport Serious Offenders', undated (accessed 07 August 2026)

policies.statement: Introduce benefits stand-down for first years of residence visa

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that disruptive students can be a risk to the safety of other students and teaching staff, distracting others from learning during valuable teaching time.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would amend legislation so that teachers have an explicit legal power to direct a seriously or persistently disruptive student to leave and go to a staffed, supervised space. A refusal would be escalated to a dean or senior leader. If the student refused again after escalation, staff would be able to use reasonable force to remove them. The current Act would be clarified to allow reasonable and proportionate intervention to prevent harm or the destruction of property. Parents could be fined and authorities involved if they do not attend meetings with their child.

citations.title: 'Disrupt the Class, Leave the Class', undated (accessed 11 August 2026)

policies.statement: Give teachers legal powers to remove disruptive students from class

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that migrants who come to NZ should have a solid base-level understanding of the country's most-used language. By ensuring greater English language proficiency, the party promises to increase public trust in the immigration system.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would extend existing English language requirements to all Accredited Employer Work Visa candidates. It would  exempt seasonal workers.

citations.title: 'Deport Serious Offenders', undated (accessed 07 August 2026)

policies.statement: Apply English language requirements for accredited employer work visas

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that emission reduction targets and the emissions trading scheme (ETS) are too costly for New Zealanders. The party cites that trading partners and competitors are not making the same commitments. Additionally, the party cites failed auctions for carbon credits due to purchasing carbon being too expensive under the ETS.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would repeal the Zero Carbon Act that commits NZ to net zero by 2050. Instead, the party claims that it would tie the emissions cap to the average of NZ's major trading partners. The party would also cut the government's price floor in the ETS. This would lower the costs of carbon emissions for polluting firms.

citations.title: 'Scrap Net Zero, Cut the Carbon Tax' (PDF), 6 September 2026 (accessed 07 September 2026)
'Only ACT will cut the Carbon Tax', 8 September 2026 (accessed 11 September 2026)

policies.statement: Cut commitments, legislation and measures that lower emissions

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that revenue from the emissions trading scheme is just another means by which the government raises revenue, and damages business competitiveness. The party seeks instead to refund the revenue generated to New Zealanders. The party additionally seeks to support businesses most affected by competitiveness concerns. The party is also concerned with the construction of carbon forests as an inefficient use of land.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: The party would refund revenue derived from ETS auctions to citizens. Industrial carbon assistance would be raised to 90 percent and 60 percent rates where businesses face carbon-cost disadvantages.  The party would remove mandates for carbon forests, with the intention to use that land for farming instead.

citations.title: 'Scrap Net Zero, Cut the Carbon Tax' (PDF), 6 September 2026 (accessed 07 September 2026)
'Only ACT will cut the Carbon Tax', 8 September 2026 (accessed 11 September 2026)
'Carbon auction farce why ACT will cut the Carbon Tax', 7 September 2026 (accessed 11 September 2026)

policies.statement: Increase support for businesses and households affected by the emissions trading scheme

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that some businesses depend on migrant workers, creating a barrier to employment for New Zealanders. Adding an automatic expiry to accredited employer visas and requiring evidence of sustained need from the employer would ensure businesses hire New Zealanders when possible.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would add a 12-month expiration date to the accredited employer visa. For a migrant worker to remain eligible, the employer would need to provide up-to-date evidence of demand.

citations.title: 'Deport Serious Offenders', undated (accessed 07 August 2026)

policies.statement: Add annual expiry dates to accredited employer visas

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that there are as many as 20,980 known overstayers in NZ. Platform apps like Uber and DoorDash do not require evidence of work rights for their drivers, which are needed irrespective of employment status. It is concerned that platform apps can encourage illegal overstaying.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would establish a dedicated overstayer enforcement unit within Immigration New Zealand. Platform employers such as Uber and DoorDash would be required to verify and report work rights. Employers who facilitate overstaying would lose accreditation.

citations.title: 'Deport Serious Offenders', undated (accessed 07 August 2026)

policies.statement: Make Uber and DoorDash-like platform companies provide evidence of work rights

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that there is a lack of reporting of rural crime in NZ. It attributes this to a lack of trust in whether police will investigate. The prosecution rate is presently at 15%.  The lack of enforcement encourages rural crime.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would provide additional funding to expand the 111 service and hire more officers for rural areas, with a target of an additional 100,000 extra patrol hours each year. It would establish a dedicated rural crime unit.

citations.title: 'Rural Crime Crackdown', undated (accessed 07 August 2026)
'ACT will drive down costs for farmers', 22 October 2026 (accessed 23 October 2026)

policies.statement: Expand rural policing

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that treaty and cultural standards as both unnecessary and an improper rationale for disciplinary action. The party is concerned that standards can encroach deeply personal individual views on contentious political matters.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would ban professional regulators from disciplining members for lawful expression outside their professional practice. It says this would protect free speech and expression. It would require regulators to remain institutionally neutral on political and ideological issues. Mandatory training would be restricted to matters directly connected to professional competence and public safety, and there would be judicial oversight so courts could rein in regulators that went beyond their legal powers.

citations.title: 'Free Speech for Regulated Professionals', undated (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Prevent professionals from being disciplined for expressing opinions outside of their practice

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that following the completion of the treaty settlement process, reparations for treaty violations by the Crown would be complete. It describes the ongoing influence of the Waitangi Tribunal on current government decisions as overreach by the courts over democratically elected political leaders.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would amend the Treaty of Waitangi Act so that the Tribunal is automatically disestablished once all eligible historical claims have been completed. Once all settlements and claims lodged by the existing statutory deadline of 1 September 2008 are completed, the Waitangi Tribunal should be disestablished. The party argues that redress should be final so the country can move forward, leaving past grievances behind.

citations.title: 'Finish the settlements, wind up the Waitangi Tribunal', 10 September 2026 (accessed 11 September 2026)

policies.statement: Abolish the Waitangi Tribunal once historical claims are resolved

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says infrastructure should have its funding protected so that governments cannot redirect its revenue for other purposes. People have paid the fuel tax expecting it to fund the road infrastructure they use, as opposed to other priorities. Mana Whenua considerations, non-functional art, monuments, and decorative amenities on roads should also be excluded for this same reason.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would legislate that the National Land Transport Fund be used only for road-related infrastructure. The party would also amend procurement rules to not favour any group over another.

citations.title: 'Keep New Zealand Moving' (PDF), 4 September 2026 (accessed 11 September 2026)

policies.statement: Focus National Land Transport Fund on road infrastructure only

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that potential infrastructure projects, when seeking approval, should be required to publish a lowest-cost safe option alongside the preferred option. Both options should include cost, delivery time, and benefit-cost ratio for each. The party says this is to assess whether the preferred design is taking unnecessary steps or being made with overly conservative assumptions.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would mandate affordability and efficacy standards, made through the comparison with a cheaper alternative design, be applied to all infrastructure projects seeking government approval.

citations.title: 'Keep New Zealand Moving' (PDF), 4 September 2026 (accessed 11 September 2026)

policies.statement: Require infrastructure projects to consider a cheaper option

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that councils are responsible for housing developments, while central government is responsible for state highways. Because of these different priorities, housing projects can occur without central government having to build the road capacity to deal with the increased growth. This worsens traffic, travel times and bus networks.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would require major growth areas to have funded transport-capacity plans. These plans would guarantee funding mechanisms such as road charges, tolls, developer contributions, council funding and private capital to ensure road capacity keeps up with population growth.

citations.title: 'Keep New Zealand Moving' (PDF), 4 September 2026 (accessed 11 September 2026)

policies.statement: Require major growth areas to have funded transport-capacity plans

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that regulations for used cars being imported into NZ can push up costs for people and families needing to buy a car. Import passenger registrations have fallen from around 165,000 in 2017 to 85,000 as people increasingly keep their current car for longer, putting off upgrading to newer, safer models.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would introduce an affordability test for imported cars. This test would flag a regulation if it is seen to reduce supply, thus increasing the prices of used cars.

citations.title: 'Keep New Zealand Moving' (PDF), 4 September 2026 (accessed 11 September 2026)

policies.statement: Introduce an affordability test on used-car import regulations

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that higher minimum wages can decrease the demand from businesses for workers to employ. The subsequent unemployment disproportionately burdens young people.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would freeze the minimum wage at its current rate for three years. This would cause the minimum wage to lose value due to inflation,  allowing more headroom in budgets for employers to bring on more staff, including younger people.

citations.title: 'Let small business get on with business' (PDF), 15 September 2026 (accessed 15 September 2026)

policies.statement: Freeze the minimum wage for three years

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the minimum wage can increase wage costs at the expense of employing someone new. Young people are less experienced and more likely to struggle to find a job. Younger workers have less experience, need more training and are more costly to hire.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would establish a training wage at 60 per cent of the adult minimum wage for workers under 20, available for their first 12 months with an employer. Standard protections would still apply with the new lower wage rate.

citations.title: 'Let small business get on with business' (PDF), 15 September 2026 (accessed 15 September 2026)

policies.statement: Introduce a training wage

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that employers can worry about discussing the end of an employment relationship. The party also says that once a 90-day period has passed, employers should be able to move on without fear of personal grievances being taken up against them for workers they have stopped employing.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would allow protected employment exit negotiations. It would limit the time to take a personal grievance to the Employment Relations Authority to 90 days after it is raised, while retaining the existing rules for sexual-harassment grievances.

citations.title: 'Let small business get on with business' (PDF), 15 September 2026 (accessed 15 September 2026)

policies.statement: Protect employers from personal grievances

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that that the relationship between a union and its members is a private association between them and does not concern the employer.  It is unreasonable to expect union fees to be collected through payroll deductions administered by the employer.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would ensure that employers were not made by law to facilitate the financial relationship between unions and members. Unions would have the ability to set up their own financial capacity through online banking instead.

citations.title: 'Let small business get on with business' (PDF), 15 September 2026 (accessed 15 September 2026)

policies.statement: Make unions collect their own fees

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the way Inland Revenue allows the deduction of business costs that come from software platforms varies inconsistently. This disadvantages businesses and technology platforms.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would review current depreciation and business expense rules to simplify how software and digital investments are treated.

citations.title: 'Let small business get on with business' (PDF), 15 September 2026 (accessed 15 September 2026)

policies.statement: Reevaluate the tax treatment of software and digital investment

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that NZ should play its part to reduce emissions but only in line with what other trading partners do, so that the country is not at a competitive disadvantage. The net zero target is arbitrary, and emissions reductions should be weighted in terms of trade.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would repeal the current Zero Carbon Act and adopted a trade-weighted approach to emissions reduction instead. The net zero by 2050 goal would be removed, and New Zealand would only do what its trading partners are doing.  This party would also protect NZ workers at risk of losing their jobs in high-emissions industries like steel production, so that these industries face lower carbon prices or none at all and are not at a competitive disadvantage.

citations.title: 'Scrap Net Zero, Cut the Carbon Tax' (PDF), 6 September 2026 (accessed 07 September 2026)
'ACT will make farming fun again ', 20 September 2026 (accessed 21 September 2026)
'ACT will drive down costs for farmers', 22 October 2026 (accessed 23 October 2026)

policies.statement: Repeal the Zero Carbon Act and NZ's net zero goal

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS) acts as a "carbon tax", with a minimum price for carbon credits set by the government. This means the auctions do not work properly and raises the price of goods and services. The supply of carbon credits should be increased and the profit returned as a refund to New Zealanders.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would remove the price floor from the Emissions Trading Scheme to place downward pressure on the carbon price. 100 percent of the money from the carbon auction would be returned to New Zealanders as a tax refund. If the amount became so low that the refund was impractical to deliver, it would mean prices had fallen so that people had lower prices for goods and services and would no longer need the tax refund.  Conversions of farmland to permanent forest for creating carbon credits would be discouraged.

citations.title: 'Scrap Net Zero, Cut the Carbon Tax' (PDF), 6 September 2026 (accessed 07 September 2026)
'ACT will drive down costs for farmers', 22 October 2026 (accessed 23 October 2026)

policies.statement: Remove the carbon price floor and return ETS profits to households

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that many of the changes required to reduce emissions can be provided by novel technology rather than the emissions trading scheme or similar financial systems. To protect prosperity, it says there should be fewer barriers for people to invest in new technologies, especially those which may reduce emissions.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would continue to oppose any new financial penalties for carbon emissions. It would remove regulations that it says prevent people from investing in new technology with potential emission-reduction benefits.

citations.title: 'Scrap Net Zero, Cut the Carbon Tax' (PDF), 6 September 2026 (accessed 07 September 2026)
'ACT will make farming fun again ', 20 September 2026 (accessed 21 September 2026)
'ACT will drive down costs for farmers', 22 October 2026 (accessed 23 October 2026)

policies.statement: Reduce emissions with a focus on new technology

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that emissions-focused regulation worries farmers who are concerned with industry competitiveness in global export markets. The party argues that the government is getting in the way of decisions that should be made by farmers, and that they should be supported in leading environmental protections, since they have a vested interest in the preservation of their land.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would omit agriculture from climate-related legislation such as the Zero Carbon Act and Emissions Trading Scheme. The party has supported reforms to the Resource Management Act, shifting funding from Te Mana o te Wai to rural catchment groups, increasing funding for rural catchment groups, allowing targeted grazing on suitable DOC land, and continuing the war against wilding pines.

citations.title: 'ACT will make farming fun again ', 20 September 2026 (accessed 21 September 2026)
'ACT will drive down costs for farmers', 22 October 2026 (accessed 23 October 2026)

policies.statement: Ensure agriculture is not included in emission reduction programmes

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that neighborhoods are frustrated by loud vehicles late at night. It notes that families are woken up by loud noises and are stressed about how such noise affects their sleep or the sleep of young children.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would introduce noise-detecting cameras in place of present police officers. These cameras would feature microphones, video and number plate recognition. They would measure the sound generated by passing vehicles, identify which vehicle produced it, and record the evidence needed for enforcement. This change would model similar systems in New York, London, and Taiwan. It would amend existing legislation to introduce the penalty and that the fine for noise charges would be $300. This party estimates that this policy would cost a one-off $2 million.

citations.title: 'ACT will protect the peace, crack down on noisy vehicles', 26 September 2026 (accessed 28 September 2026)
'Crack Down on Noisy Vehicles' (PDF), 26 September 2026 (accessed 28 September 2026)

policies.statement: Introduce noise-detecting cameras

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that NZ has often had political leadership blame companies for their prices. This creates greater bureaucracy in response, such as the recent appointment of a grocery commissioner.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would establish a one-stop body for consenting new entrants to the supermarket sector. The objective would be to reduce the consenting process from years to months. The party would additionally allow all products approved under the regulations of the United States, United Kingdom, and Australia to be automatically allowed in NZ, so it is easier for grocers to obtain various products.

citations.title: 'ACT’s plan to increase supermarket competition', 28 September 2026 (accessed 28 September 2026)

policies.statement: Create a one-stop consenting body to approve competing supermarkets

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that since 2021, New Zealanders have had the option of assisted dying, and the Ministry of Health's first statutory review recommended 25 changes to the law. The party claims that restrictions such as the six-month-to-live rule place an unnecessary barrier to access for those who remain best placed to make decisions about their own bodies.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would implement all twenty-five recommendations from the Ministry of Health report. Additionally, the six-month-to-live rule would be replaced by a test based on whether a person's condition is advanced, progressive, and expected to cause death.

citations.title: 'Strengthening End of Life Choice', undated (accessed 29 September 2026)
'ACT commits to strengthening end-of-life choice', 5 August 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)

policies.statement: Remove the "six months" caveat for assisted dying

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that there's a lack of competition in the energy sector. However, independent analysis commissioned by the government found no material competition problem requiring the break-up of the major generator-retailers. Instead, the party says regulatory barriers are the key driver of the cost of power. Encouraging people to sell excess power would reward people who invest their own money in generation and storage.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would allow people with excess power, often from solar installed on their house, to sell their excess power. The selling of excess power would be done by businesses and community energy schemes, subject to appropriate metering, network charging and consumer protections.

citations.title: 'Stability, investment, affordability: The keys to abundant electricity' (PDF), 18 September 2026 (accessed 29 September 2026)

policies.statement: Encourage people generating power to sell it to the grid

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that regulatory barriers lift the cost of power for New Zealanders. Allowing private businesses to access the national grid can increase capital investment in energy production, helping to lower costs over time.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would allow for private firms to finance and build transmission lines connected to the national grid.   To do so, these businesses would have to prove that they meet common technical and reliability standards and have adequate coordination with a system operator.

citations.title: 'Stability, investment, affordability: The keys to abundant electricity' (PDF), 18 September 2026 (accessed 29 September 2026)

policies.statement: Open power transmission to private investment

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that already existing power line companies allow consumers to choose the contractor responsible for connecting their land or property to the power grid. The party says greater consumer choice is preferable to some customers to find themselves locked into a single provider.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would establish an accreditation process for contractors who wish to enter the market for the connection of land/housing to power lines. The party claims that this process will better allow power line companies to offer more choice in contractors for their consumers.

citations.title: 'Stability, investment, affordability: The keys to abundant electricity' (PDF), 18 September 2026 (accessed 29 September 2026)

policies.statement: Establish an accreditation process for contractors to connect households to the power grid

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that network upgrades for power can be costly for households. Alternative options for consumers should be available as cheaper alternatives to upgrades.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would require material network reinforcement projects done by power line companies to demonstrate that credible alternatives have been properly considered when tending to customer-funded network upgrades. Such alternatives under consideration would include batteries, demand response, flexible connections, local generation and other technologies competing against conventional poles, wires and substations.

citations.title: 'Stability, investment, affordability: The keys to abundant electricity' (PDF), 18 September 2026 (accessed 29 September 2026)

policies.statement: Mandate consideration of alternatives to power network upgrades

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that proposals to emulate Australia's social-media ban for under-sixteen-year-olds come with privacy concerns. The party argues that the recent settlement between the United States and Meta (Facebook, Instagram) provides a better framework for dealing with the harm experienced by children due to social media.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would ask Parliament to investigate forming a similar settlement with Meta which would include changes seen in the United States. Changes would include a default two-hour daily limit for teenagers, locking most teen accounts between midnight and 6 am, switching off push notifications overnight and during school hours, and giving parents greater power to supervise and restrict their children’s accounts. Teenagers would also need parental approval to loosen the main restrictions.

citations.title: 'Landmark social media settlement shows better way forward', 27 August 2026 (accessed 29 September 2026)

policies.statement: Commission Parliament to explore a deal with Meta for young people on social media

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that Auckland Grammar does not have the capacity to meet the growing demand across the Epsom area. It cites advocacy from the principals of Auckland Grammar School and Epsom Girls’ Grammar School for a new co-ed school in this area.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would purchase land from the University of Auckland and its Epsom campus and repurpose the facility into a co-ed high school. Parents would retain eligibility for the grammar school's school zone.

citations.title: 'Campaign launched to acquire land for new school in Epsom', 1 October 2026 (accessed 02 October 2026)

policies.statement: Acquire land for a new school in Epsom

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that spiritual beliefs, particularly those that come from Te Ao Māori, should not be used as the basis for assessing an infrastructure project's viability. It says that planning law should regulate effects that can be identified, measured and tested, and protect rights recognised by law. It should not require planners, councils or judges to rule on spiritual or religious beliefs.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would exclude purely spiritual and religious effects. It would legislate that a religious or spiritual belief, or a claim of spiritual harm, could not on its own be treated as an adverse effect or justify refusing or restricting consent, requesting further information, or imposing a consent condition. The rule would apply equally to all religions and belief systems and use the test already applied under the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act. It would also ban compulsory spiritual observances. No consent or permit could require anyone to perform, take part in, arrange or fund a prayer, karakia, blessing or other religious observance. Anyone who wants to do these things voluntarily could still do so.

citations.title: 'Leave spirituality out of infrastructure', 3 October 2026 (accessed 05 October 2026)

policies.statement: Exclude purely spiritual and religious effects from infrastructure planning law

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that compulsory karaka and religious prayer required for consenting processes should be removed, as the compulsion element violates the individual right to abstain from cultural practices should they choose. The party says that people should be able to abstain without losing a consent.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would remove cultural practice requirements from consenting processes. The party says that all protections that exist for heritage sites, urupā, archaeological sites, customary physical uses, water quality, ecosystems and rights in Treaty settlement legislation, outside of consent processes, will remain untouched.

citations.title: 'Leave spirituality out of infrastructure', 3 October 2026 (accessed 05 October 2026)

policies.statement: Remove the use of spiritual practices like karakia during consenting

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the current water standards under the newly introduced government water management entity are too vague its objectives. It says that the standards focus too greatly on 'spiritual' criteria.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would replace current standards with a sole focus on measurable freshwater outcomes and remove Te Ao Māori-related concerns.

citations.title: 'Leave spirituality out of infrastructure', 3 October 2026 (accessed 05 October 2026)
'ACT will drive down costs for farmers', 22 October 2026 (accessed 23 October 2026)

policies.statement: Replace Te Mana o te Wai with measurable freshwater outcomes

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that New Zealanders deserve to keep more of their money for their own retirement. The party argues that the tax made from KiwiSaver is used to top up those with low incomes who have small savings. The party says that people's savings will increase without having to put additional money away for their retirement.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would remove the government contribution to KiwiSaver to fund the exemption of KiwiSaver from taxation. The party claims they will put rules in place to avoid people using KiwiSaver as a tax shelter.  This party estimates that this policy would cost just under $2.4 billion over four years.

citations.title: 'No tax on KiwiSaver earnings' (PDF), 4 October 2026 (accessed 05 October 2026)

policies.statement: Do not tax KiwiSaver earnings

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that New Zealand needs to produce energy through mineral extraction. Extraction takes a long time between the initial investment and the returns, and investors need confidence that consent process will remain in place.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would establish a statutory body to ensure compensation for investors in mineral extraction. Any future government would be required to pay compensation to investors if permit rights are withdrawn. It would facilitate this by adding property rights into the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act and ensuring that any legal challenge opposing a permit does not suspend that permit.

citations.title: 'Unlocking Mineral and Energy Wealth' (PDF), 8 October 2026 (accessed 08 October 2026)

policies.statement: Establish a statutory body to ensure compensation for investors in mineral extraction

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that New Zealand's economy would benefit from more jobs in resource and mineral extraction, and the government would gain from increased royalty payments.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would guarantee regular updates to the Crown Mineral List, establish national policy direction and standards for mines, quarries and mineral processing under the new planning legislation, retain fast-track access for eligible projects, and have government work alongside industry to build up the workforce in extractive industries.

citations.title: 'Unlocking Mineral and Energy Wealth' (PDF), 8 October 2026 (accessed 08 October 2026)

policies.statement: Create a set of national mineral extractions standards

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that global energy markets are becoming more competitive. Expanding domestic energy production could bring commercial and security benefits for New Zealand and allied nations.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would continue to allow offshore gas exploration. It would encourage businesses to use renewable energy or fossil fuels with no preference for either option. It would revise the Crown Minerals Act to create rules for underground gas storage . It would also support LNG (gas) import infrastructure as insurance against changes in NZ's domestic gas production.

citations.title: 'Unlocking Mineral and Energy Wealth' (PDF), 8 October 2026 (accessed 08 October 2026)

policies.statement: Expand domestic energy production

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that regulatory barriers can create increased costs for investors and firms engaged in mining and gas and oil extraction. Regulations that duplicate criteria that are already met waste time, money and state resources.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would have separate legislation around mining with the goal of minimising similar regulations. One piece of legislation would focus on the allocation of Crown-owned petroleum and minerals, another on the management of environmental effects and another on consenting processes.

citations.title: 'Unlocking Mineral and Energy Wealth' (PDF), 8 October 2026 (accessed 08 October 2026)

policies.statement: Revise legislation for resource extraction

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that clear rules are needed for responsible mining, to ensure that resource extraction is done without tax money being used to deal with preventable environmental damage. However, extraction companies should be able to follower fewer regulations if they can demonstrate that there is less risk to the environment.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would target marine protection at significant ecological features, including important seamounts, habitats and breeding areas. The party says it would give regulators the discretion to allow, in the case of unanticipated effects, the reduction of regulations where evidence demonstrates a lower risk.

citations.title: 'Unlocking Mineral and Energy Wealth' (PDF), 8 October 2026 (accessed 08 October 2026)

policies.statement: Increase the flexibility around environmental regulations for mining

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that New Zealanders should be encouraged to donate to charity. Charities across New Zealand help people. The $33,333 cap on tax benefits for money spent on charitable donations should be removed so that people donate more money to charity. This would encourage the philanthropic sector to partner with the government to deliver services, such as a proposal to create cancer treatment centres in Auckland and Christchurch.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would remove the $33,333 cap on tax rebates for money spent on charitable donations.

citations.title: 'ACT will remove the cap on generosity', 7 October 2026 (accessed 08 October 2026)

policies.statement: Remove the cap on tax deductions for charitable donations

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that its leader was disappointed that the Minister of Education confirmed that Agricultural and Horticultural Science won't remain as a standalone subject in the Year 11 Science curriculum. It says that 63% of the over 100,000 students who took the subject last year were from urban schools and argues that students should have access to a subject tailored to building knowledge in agriculture, a major export industry.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would keep Agricultural and Horticultural Science as a standalone subject in Year 11.

citations.title: 'Keep agriculture in the curriculum', 9 October 2026 (accessed 09 October 2026)
'ACT will drive down costs for farmers', 22 October 2026 (accessed 23 October 2026)

policies.statement: Keep agriculture as a subject in the Year 11 curriculum

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that NZ is under pressure to tighten its belt and reduce government spending. The party views foreign aid spending as needing to be cut to instead prioritise domestic issues and reducing debt.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would direct the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade to reduce foreign aid spending back to 2017 levels. The party claims that this would result in annual savings of $283 million. Money being given to Ukraine would be excluded from this reduction.

citations.title: 'New Zealand can't keep exporting taxpayers' money  ', 10 October 2026 (accessed 12 October 2026)

policies.statement: Reduce NZ's foreign aid to 2017 levels

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that its ambition is to reach a budget surplus earlier without raising taxes, and that savings increase over time. It claims that what starts as saving $400 million will become $1.6 billion annually by 2030/31.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would reduce new government spending by reducing future operating allowances in government budgets over the next four years.  This party estimates that this policy would save a total $1.6 billion over four years..

citations.title: 'Act Fiscal Plan 2026' (PDF), 11 October 2026 (accessed 12 October 2026)

policies.statement: Reduce new government spending from $2.4 billion to $2 billion

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that issues of duplication arise from ministries tasked with analysing policy impacts on various demographic groups. It says that this analysis is already being done by the ministries and government departments overseeing the delivery of services.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would abolish all demographic groups ministries. The party is not clear on whether that includes the Ministry for Māori Development's role in helping the government manage the Māori economy, not just the analysis of inquiries between Māori and non-Māori service users. This party estimates that this policy would cost save $187 million annually.

citations.title: 'Act Fiscal Plan 2026' (PDF), 11 October 2026 (accessed 12 October 2026)

policies.statement: Abolish demographic group ministries

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that increased life expectancy and lowered birthrates mean taxes need to rise to keep up with population ageing. The party wishes to raise the eligibility age of superannuation by three months a year, reaching 67 by 2035.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would legislate the eligibility age for NZ superannuation be raised 3 months every year until 2035 where the age would reach 67. The party additionally would suspend government payments into the NZ Superannuation Fund. This party estimates that this policy would cost $2.4 billion after four years.

citations.title: 'Act Fiscal Plan 2026' (PDF), 11 October 2026 (accessed 12 October 2026)

policies.statement: Raise the retirement age to 67 by 2035

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that independent/private schools provide diversity and choice in NZ’s schooling system. Parents should have greater choice of school options.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would align/index the independent school subsidy to the increases made to the public school operations grant.  This party estimates that this policy would cost $100 million total over four years.

citations.title: 'Act Fiscal Plan 2026' (PDF), 11 October 2026 (accessed 12 October 2026)

policies.statement: Increase private school subsidies in line with public school operations

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that financial education should be practical and feel relevant to young people. It says that giving a small $500 investment to Year 11 students would give teenagers a reason to engage with saving, risk and business ownership, especially for those who would not encounter investing at home.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would establish a fund that would provide Year 11 students with a deposit of $500, accompanied by a financial literacy program in school. Students would be allowed to invest the money and would graduate with an understanding. The investment could move from low-risk bank deposits to investing in funds, to higher-risk investments in individual businesses (equities).  This party estimates that this policy would cost $35 million annually.

citations.title: 'Act Fiscal Plan 2026' (PDF), 11 October 2026 (accessed 12 October 2026)

policies.statement: Give high school students money to teach them how to invest

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that increasing costs on landlords may be passed onto renters, lifting the cost of housing. The party says that landlords renting out commercial property can reduce taxable income to offset losses from their rental, but a reform from the previous Labour government means that at present, residential landlords cannot. The party wishes to change that.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would allow residential landlords to offset losses from rental properties against their other income, reducing their overall tax rate. Bringing the tax rules for residential landlords in line with those for commercial landlords. This party estimates that this policy would cost $1.14 billion over four years.

citations.title: 'ACT to abolish another of Labour's renters' taxes', 14 October 2026 (accessed 14 October 2026)
'Act Fiscal Plan 2026' (PDF), 11 October 2026 (accessed 12 October 2026)

policies.statement: Allow residential landlords to reduce taxable income to offset losses

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that Hauraki Gulf Marine Park needs to have its own catchment area. Instead of the status quo, where rules apply to a much larger area.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would create a fishery area for the smaller Hauraki Gulf Marine Park where the total allowable catch could be adjusted to sustainable levels. Whatever proportion of the quota present holders have would be maintained if the total allowable catch were to fall. For example, one would retain an entitlement to 5%.

citations.title: 'Unlocking New Zealand’s Fishing Potential' (PDF), 30 August 2026 (accessed 14 October 2026)

policies.statement: Establish a Hauraki Gulf marine area

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that rock pools around Auckland have increasingly faced intensive harvesting of shellfish and other marine life. Patches of rock pools no longer have much life remaining and are being overused. The party says such an issue of overfishing is common across NZ.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would introduce a nationwide combined recreational daily bag limit of 10 for shellfish and other covered species that do not already have their own individual daily limit. Shellfish with individual catch limits would have those catch limits remain unchanged.

citations.title: 'Unlocking New Zealand’s Fishing Potential' (PDF), 30 August 2026 (accessed 14 October 2026)

policies.statement: Create daily limits on harvesting from Auckland rock pools

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that practice of scallop dredging damages the seabed, so that fisheries can be closed down to recover. Alternative harvesting methods exist, so the particular method of scallop dredging is not needed.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would permanently ban scallop dredging in scallop fisheries that are currently closed. It would allow selective harvesting technologies as stock numbers recover.

citations.title: 'Unlocking New Zealand’s Fishing Potential' (PDF), 30 August 2026 (accessed 14 October 2026)

policies.statement: Bad scallop dredging

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that existing conservation levies from the fisheries regulator, Fisheries NZ, do not account for the differences in environmental damage that different methods of catching can cause. This issue means taxpayers and other users can be burdened with costs imposed by others. The party is also concerned that present fees are not punitive enough to discourage poor practice.

attributes.name: How
